texts: The banding is consistent with seasonal deposition in the lake basin.
Shell fragments are articulated, so the bivalves were buried alive.
Grain sorting in the sandstone points to a low-energy setting.
The ostracod assemblage shows no sign of reworking or predation.
The varve count gives roughly four hundred laminae in the sandstone.
Bioturbation is absent, so burrowing fauna never colonized the bed.
Magnetic susceptibility drops sharply across the clay lamina.
Fish scales are concentrated in one horizon with intact fin rays.
Cross-bedding in the sandstone shows a consistent paleocurrent.
Pollen in the shell bed is dominated by one conifer taxon.
The clay lamina has an erosional base cutting the sandstone.
Juvenile shells outnumber adults, which suggests a mass mortality.

paraphrase: Arguably, the horizon assays at 18.4 ppm iridium.
That said, I think the grain diameter is 212.7 microns, roughly.
Perhaps the varve count is about 400, to some extent consistent with seasonal deposition.
In fairness, the core has 3.1 percent organic carbon.
Broadly speaking, shell counts reach 57.0 per kilogram.
It's worth noting the susceptibility is 142.7 SI units.
